templates.title: Rate-limit rejections by limit type, per model and spend tier as of each request
templates.subtopic: as-of join to a slowly changing tier, deduplication, conditional aggregation

sections.scenario: A model API enforces two limits per model for each team: requests per second and tokens per minute. Both grow with the team's spend tier, and a team moves up a tier when its cumulative spend crosses a threshold (this exercise's tiers; check current docs). A rejected request gets HTTP 429, and the gateway logs which limit it hit. Developers keep asking whether they are mostly hitting the request limit or the token limit, and whether that changes after an upgrade. You are asked for the split per model and tier, where the tier is the one the team was on when it sent the request, not the one it is on today.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query over tier_changes(team_id, tier, effective_at) and request_log(log_id, gateway, request_id, team_id, model, requested_at, status_code, limit_hit) that returns model, tier, requests, rps_rejections, tpm_rejections, rps_share, tpm_share: one row per model and tier with at least one request, ordered by model, tier. A request's tier is the tier of its team's latest tier_changes row with effective_at at or before requested_at (a row applies from its effective_at, inclusive). requests counts requests; rps_rejections and tpm_rejections count requests with status 429 whose limit_hit is 'rps' or 'tpm'; the two shares are those counts over requests, each rounded to 4 decimal places. {{status_rule}} {{tier_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{requests}} requests in {{log_rows}} log rows. Every 429 has a limit_hit; every other status has limit_hit NULL.
sections.assumptions: Model names, tiers, team names and every number are hypothetical, and the tiers here are this exercise's rule, not any product's real thresholds or limits; check current docs. Teams are reported only in aggregate. All timestamps are UTC.
sections.criteria: Tier taken as of requested_at with the boundary inclusive; one row per request before aggregating (Very Hard); teams on tier 1 before their first row (Very Hard); only 429s counted as rejections and split by limit_hit, other errors kept in the denominator (Hard+); correct rounding with numeric division; deterministic order; can discuss before/after comparisons, headroom and scale.

clarifications.q: Which tier does a request sent at the very second of an upgrade belong to?
clarifications.a: The new one. A tier row applies from its effective_at, inclusive.

clarifications.q: Do tiers ever go down?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; cumulative spend only grows. Your query should not rely on that, though: take the latest row at or before the request.

clarifications.q: Is a 503 a rejection?
clarifications.a: No. Only status 429 is a rate-limit rejection. Other failures are still requests and stay in the denominator.

clarifications.q: How are shares rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(count::numeric / requests, 4), half away from zero.

clarifications.q: Should models or tiers with no requests appear?
clarifications.a: No. Only (model, tier) pairs with at least one request.

hints: Settle the grain first: one row per request. Then attach the tier, then aggregate.
The tier as of a time is "the latest row at or before it": a correlated subquery with ORDER BY effective_at DESC LIMIT 1, a LATERAL join, or DISTINCT ON after a range join.
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status_code = 429 AND limit_hit = 'rps') keeps both splits in one pass.
followups: Developers say an upgrade did not help. How would you compare each team's rejection rate in the days before and after its upgrade without mixing teams of different sizes?
Token limits are per minute and request limits per second. How would you show how close a model ran to each limit, not just how often it was hit?
The log is billions of rows a day. How would you partition it and maintain the tier as of each request without an as-of join over the whole history?

A tier change is recorded in the billing system and reaches the gateways within minutes (this exercise's rule). How would you measure requests rejected under the old tier after the new one took effect?

rules.ask: You attached the team's tier as it is today. What happens to a request sent last week, before the upgrade?
How does this as-of lookup behave for a team with thousands of tier rows, and what index makes it cheap?
You turned tier rows into ranges with LEAD. Is the upper bound inclusive or exclusive, and what happens at the exact second of an upgrade?
Two gateways logged the same request. Which columns decide that two rows are the same request, and which row do you keep?
Is every failed request a rate-limit rejection? Where do 500s and 503s go in your numbers?

templates.title: Batch turnaround per size band and week, with batches still pending at the window shown apart
templates.subtopic: composite-key joins, per-batch rollups, ordered-set percentiles with FILTER

sections.scenario: Teams submit batches of model requests for asynchronous processing. Each request inside a batch carries an id the team chose itself (custom_id), and results come back one by one as they finish. This exercise's completion window is {{window_hours}} hours from submission (check current docs for any real product's window). The platform wants a weekly view of how long batches really take, by batch size, and how many requests got a result within the window, without letting a few stuck batches distort the typical turnaround.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query over batches(batch_id, team_id, submitted_at), batch_requests(batch_id, custom_id) and batch_results(result_id, batch_id, custom_id, result_at, outcome) that returns week_start, size_band, batches, requests, in_window_share, pending_batches, median_hours, one row per week and size band with at least one batch, ordered by week_start, size_band. week_start is the date of the Monday (UTC) of the week of submitted_at. A batch's size is its number of batch_requests rows; size_band is 1 for sizes 1 to {{mid_less}}, {{mid}} for {{mid}} to {{large_less}}, and {{large}} for {{large}} or more. A request is in window when it has a result at or before submitted_at plus {{window_hours}} hours; an errored result is still a result. in_window_share is in-window requests over all requests in the group, rounded to 4 places. A batch is pending at the window if any of its requests is not in window; pending_batches counts them. For every other batch, its turnaround is the time from submitted_at to its last result; median_hours is the median turnaround of those batches in hours, rounded to 2 places, where the median is the lower middle value for an even count (percentile_disc(0.5)), or NULL if every batch in the group was pending. {{id_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{batches}} batches. Join results to requests on the full key (batch_id, custom_id).
sections.assumptions: The window, size bands, teams and every timestamp are hypothetical and this exercise's rule; check current docs. Result content is never read: only times and the outcome label. All times are UTC.
sections.criteria: Results joined on (batch_id, custom_id) (Hard+); requests with no result kept and counted as not in window; the window inclusive; errored results counted as results; pending batches excluded from the median and counted apart; a request's earliest result used (Very Hard); correct band boundaries and Monday weeks; deterministic order; can discuss request-level percentiles, cancellations and incremental maintenance.

clarifications.q: Is a result exactly at the window's end in window?
clarifications.a: Yes. The window is inclusive: result_at <= submitted_at + interval.

clarifications.q: Why leave pending batches out of the median?
clarifications.a: Their last result is either missing or after the window, so their turnaround is unknown or censored. They are reported in pending_batches instead.

clarifications.q: Does an errored result count?
clarifications.a: Yes. The request was answered within the window; whether it succeeded is a different report.

clarifications.q: Which week does a batch submitted Sunday 23:58 UTC belong to?
clarifications.a: The week starting the Monday before. Weeks start Monday 00:00 UTC.

clarifications.q: Is the turnaround computed from in-window results only?
clarifications.a: It is only computed for batches whose every request is in window, so the last result is in the window too.

hints: Build one row per request with its result time (or NULL) first, then one row per batch, then aggregate per week and band.
Per batch: COUNT(*), COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE in_window), BOOL_AND(in_window) and MAX(result_at) give everything the final step needs.
Ordered-set aggregates accept a FILTER clause: percentile_disc(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …) FILTER (WHERE complete).
followups: Teams want turnaround in percentiles for the requests, not the batches. What changes, and which number is more useful to a team planning around the window?
A batch can be cancelled part way. How would you report cancelled requests without hiding them in either the in-window or the pending numbers?
Results arrive continuously for weeks of history. How would you maintain this report incrementally instead of recomputing it?
Turnaround depends on when in the day a batch was submitted. How would you show that without implying a promise the window does not make?

rules.ask: Is custom_id unique across batches? What does joining on it alone do when two teams both name their requests q1, q2, q3?
One batch took 20 times longer than the rest. What does it do to an average turnaround, and why did you choose it over the median?
percentile_cont interpolates between two batches. What does the report promise when the median is a turnaround no batch actually had?
A request with no result yet: where does it go in your query, and does its batch still appear?
Which time zone does date_trunc('week', …) use here, and what changes if a team reads this in UTC-8?

templates.title: Freshness of public posts: minutes from creation to searchable, per hour
templates.subtopic: first-event per entity, anti-filters, nearest-rank percentiles

sections.scenario: A model API offers a server-side tool that searches public posts, and the posts reach the search index through a real-time ingestion pipeline. The number that matters to developers is freshness: how long after a post is created can a search find it. Posts are rows with a given schema and no content here. Posts can be edited (each edit is a new version, indexed separately) and deleted. You are asked for hourly freshness on {{day}}, measured honestly.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query over posts(post_id, created_at, deleted_at) and searchable(post_id, version, searchable_at) that returns hour_start, posts, unsearchable, median_minutes, p95_minutes: one row per UTC hour of created_at that has at least one post that was not deleted, ordered by hour_start. Leave out every post with a deleted_at. A post's lag is the time from its created_at to the first time any of its versions became searchable (its earliest searchable_at); an edited post counts once. posts counts posts with a lag; unsearchable counts posts with no searchable row. median_minutes and p95_minutes are the 50th and 95th percentile lags by nearest rank (the value at position ceil(p · n) in ascending order, which is percentile_disc), in minutes, rounded to 2 decimal places, or NULL when the hour has no post with a lag. {{index_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{posts}} posts. Compute the percentiles on the lag before rounding.
sections.assumptions: Post ids, versions and every timestamp are synthetic, and the freshness definition is this exercise's rule; check current docs for any real product. No post content, authors or engagement are used. All times are UTC.
sections.criteria: One lag per post from its earliest searchable time across versions; deleted posts excluded from every column; posts with no searchable row counted apart and left out of the percentiles (Hard+); hours by created_at in UTC; nearest-rank percentiles on the unrounded lag; deterministic order; can discuss stage-level lag, censored posts and percentile storage.

clarifications.q: Is the lag measured to the edit's own time when the edited version is the first one searchable?
clarifications.a: No. Freshness is from the post's created_at: the post became findable at that moment, whichever version it was.

clarifications.q: Why exclude deleted posts entirely, even if they were searchable for a while?
clarifications.a: This exercise's rule: a deleted post leaves every freshness report, so a report never refers to it. Their lags can be studied elsewhere with the right controls.

clarifications.q: Which hour does a post created at 10:59:59 belong to?
clarifications.a: 10:00, the hour of created_at, even if it became searchable after 11:00.

clarifications.q: Why nearest rank instead of interpolation?
clarifications.a: So every reported percentile is a lag some post actually had, and so the number is reproducible in any engine.

hints: Reduce searchable to one row per post first: MIN(searchable_at) grouped by post_id.
Start from the posts that were not deleted and LEFT JOIN the first-searchable times, so posts with none are still counted.
percentile_disc(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM first_at - created_at)) ignores NULLs, which is exactly what unsearchable posts need.
followups: Freshness is end to end. How would you break the lag into stages (ingested, labelled, indexed, replicated) so a regression points to one stage?
A post that is never searchable has no lag. How would you report it so the percentiles do not look better as the pipeline gets worse?
Hourly percentiles cannot be added up into a daily one. How would you store data so any time range can be answered later?
At this volume, exact percentiles per hour are expensive. Which sketch would you use, and what error would you state next to the number?

rules.ask: percentile_cont interpolates. What lag does it report for an hour with five posts, and did any post have that lag?
A post was edited before its first version reached the index. When did it first become findable?
Your COUNT(*) runs after joining searchable rows. How many times does an edited post count?
You exclude deleted posts. Should a post deleted three days later be excluded from today's freshness, and what would change if it were kept?
What does one post that took 30 minutes do to an hourly average of lags that are usually under a minute?

templates.title: Fusing web and public-post search results with reciprocal rank fusion
templates.subtopic: reciprocal rank fusion with exact rational scores and deterministic ties

sections.scenario: A model can call two server-side search tools inside one response: web search and search over public posts. Each tool returns its own ranked list of sources, and the response should cite one fused list. This exercise fuses them with reciprocal rank fusion: each list contributes weight / (k + rank) to every source it contains, so a source near the top of both lists beats one that is first in only one. Both tools return canonical source ids, so a post that web search also found has the same id in both lists. The fused order must be reproducible to the last position, because citations are logged and compared across runs.
sections.problem: Implement fuse_results(web, posts, k, top_n, weights=(1, 1)). web and posts are lists of source ids, best first; a source's rank in a list is its 1-based position. A source's score is the sum, over the lists it appears in, of weight / (k + rank), with weights[0] for web and weights[1] for posts. Return the ids of at most top_n sources, highest score first; sources with equal scores are ordered by id ascending. Compare scores exactly, as fractions: two sources whose scores are equal as fractions tie, even if floating-point sums of them differ in the last bit. k is this exercise's constant ({{k}} in this instance's tests), and top_n is at least 1. {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check fuses two lists of 40 000 results each, with about a third of the post results also in the web list. Looking up each source's rank by scanning the other list is over a billion comparisons. Aim for O(n + m) work to score, plus the sort or selection of the top results.
sections.assumptions: The fusion rule, constant, weights and every list are this exercise's, hypothetical; ranking of results inside each list is a scoring function you are given, not something you compute. Ids are synthetic.
sections.criteria: 1-based ranks; one dict lookup per source per list; a repeated source counted once at its first position without renumbering (Hard+); exact score comparison with ties by id (Hard+ tests check it); integer weights handled exactly (Very Hard); top_n cut correctly inside a tie; clear complexity argument; sensible answers on more lists, canonicalisation and replay.

clarifications.q: Is rank 0-based or 1-based?
clarifications.a: 1-based: the first result has rank 1 and contributes weight / (k + 1).

clarifications.q: What if a source is missing from one list?
clarifications.a: That list contributes nothing for it. There is no penalty term.

clarifications.q: Why exact fractions? Floats are close enough.
clarifications.a: Close is not equal. Two different rank pairs can give the same fraction, and if the float sums differ in the last bit, the tie-break by id silently flips and logged citations stop matching between runs.

clarifications.q: What if there are fewer than top_n sources?
clarifications.a: Return all of them, in order.

clarifications.q: Can a source appear twice in one list?
clarifications.a: In Medium, no. In Hard and Very Hard, yes: only its first position counts, and the list is not renumbered.

hints: Build a dict from source id to its first rank, once per list. Every lookup after that is O(1).
Python's fractions.Fraction compares exactly. If you prefer integers, compare p1 * q2 with p2 * q1, or build a key from the numerator and denominator.
You only need the top top_n: heapq.nsmallest with a key of (-score, id) avoids sorting everything.
followups: A third tool joins with its own list. What changes in your code, and in the exactness argument?
One tool often returns the same page under two URLs. Where should canonicalisation happen, and what does it do to that page's rank?
Product asks for a score shown to developers. How would you present a fraction honestly, and what would you log so a fused order can be replayed?
The lists arrive as streams and the response wants the top 5 as early as possible. When can you be sure a source is in the final top 5?

rules.ask: How long does looking up one source's rank take with list.index, and how many lookups does a 40 000-result list need?
Two sources have scores equal as fractions but their float sums differ in the last bit. Which comes first in your output, and which should?
How many Fraction objects do you create, and what does each comparison cost compared with integer cross-multiplication?
You sort every source to return the top 100. What would you use instead, and when does it start to matter?
Why must the later duplicate not renumber the list, and what would renumbering do to other sources' scores?

templates.title: Merging index segments of real-time posts at the least bytes rewritten
templates.subtopic: optimal merge pattern with a min-heap, deterministic ties

sections.scenario: Public posts reach a search index in real time, so the index for {{where}} accumulates many small segments, and searches get slower as the segment count grows. A background job merges segments two at a time. A merge reads both segments and writes a new one of their combined size, so every merge rewrites bytes, and bytes rewritten are the job's main cost. The job wants a plan that brings the segment count down with the least total rewriting.
sections.problem: Implement merge_plan(segments, target=1). segments is a list of (segment_id, bytes) with distinct integer ids. Merging two segments of a and b bytes rewrites a + b bytes and replaces them with a new segment of a + b bytes; the j-th merge's new segment gets id max_id + j, where max_id is the largest id in the input. Merge until at most target segments remain. Return (total, merges): the least possible total bytes rewritten, and the plan as a list of (first_id, second_id, new_id) in order. To make the plan unique, this exercise's tie rule is that each step merges the two segments that come first by (bytes, segment_id), first_id being the one that comes first; that plan achieves the least total, and you should be ready to say why. {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check has 80 000 segments of up to 5 MB each. A plan that re-sorts the segments before every merge, or keeps a sorted list and removes from its front, does O(n) work per merge, billions of steps in total. Aim for O(n log n).
sections.assumptions: Segment sizes, ids, the cost model (rewriting is the only cost) and the target are this exercise's, hypothetical; real index merge policies weigh more than bytes. Posts and segments carry no content here.
sections.criteria: Least total bytes with the greedy two-smallest rule and a correct optimality argument; ties by (bytes, id) with new ids after every original; (0, []) for empty, single and already-small inputs (Hard+); zero-byte segments (Hard+); stop at target (Very Hard); O(n log n) with a heap or the two-queue method; sensible answers on online arrivals, f-way merges and caps.

clarifications.q: Does a merged segment's id matter?
clarifications.a: Yes: it is in the plan, and it breaks ties. It is max_id + j for the j-th merge, so it is always larger than every original id.

clarifications.q: A merged segment has the same size as an original one. Which is merged first?
clarifications.a: The one with the lower id, which is always the original.

clarifications.q: What if there are already at most target segments?
clarifications.a: No merge: return (0, []). The same for an empty list or a single segment.

clarifications.q: Can a segment have 0 bytes?
clarifications.a: In Hard and Very Hard, yes (every post in it was deleted). Merging it still counts as a merge and rewrites the other segment's bytes.

clarifications.q: Is the order of the input list meaningful?
clarifications.a: No. Only sizes and ids matter.

hints: Think about how many times each original byte is rewritten: once per merge above it. Which segments should be merged as late as possible?
Exchange argument: in any optimal plan, the two smallest segments can be merged together without increasing the total.
A min-heap of (bytes, segment_id) gives the two smallest in O(log n) and orders ties exactly as the rule asks.
followups: Prove that merging the two smallest first is optimal, including when the plan stops at target segments instead of one.
Segments keep arriving while the job runs. How would you adapt the plan, and what do you give up?
The merge can take up to f segments at once (rewriting their sum). What changes in the greedy, and when do you need zero-byte placeholders?
A merge of very large segments blocks searches on that shard. How would you cap the largest merge, and is the greedy still optimal under the cap?

rules.ask: You sort before every merge. How much work is that per merge, and for 80 000 segments in total?
insort finds the place in O(log n). What does inserting into, and popping from the front of, a Python list cost?
How does your heap order two segments of equal size, and does a merged segment ever go before an original of the same size?
Why not merge the largest segments first, to get them out of the way? Give a three-segment example.
Why are merged sizes non-decreasing, and how does that let two queues replace a heap? What happens to ties between the queues?

templates.title: Tool-call loops — the repeating cycle a server-side tool trace ends in, and how far back it reaches
templates.subtopic: Z-function of the reversed trace, periods of every suffix in one pass

sections.scenario: When a model answers with server-side tools, it chooses each next call itself: search the web, search public posts, open a result, search again. Sometimes it gets stuck and repeats the same few calls until a call budget stops it. The platform's trace analytics flags responses whose tool trace ends in such a loop and shows each team, for its own usage, which cycle repeated and from which call the loop began, so the wasted calls can be counted. Long-running agent sessions produce traces of tens of thousands of calls.
sections.problem:
Implement find_loops(traces, r, max_cycle). Each trace lists the calls of one response in the order they ran; each call is an integer id (the tool and its normalised arguments, interned earlier so that equal calls share an id). For a trace of n calls and a cycle length p, the reach of p is the number of calls at the end of the trace that repeat with period p: the largest L ≤ n such that trace[i] == trace[i + p] for every i with n − L ≤ i < n − p. The reach is always at least p.

  1. A cycle length p (from 1 to n // r) is a loop when its reach is at least r · p: at least r full copies of the last p calls end the trace. {{cap_rule}}
  2. Among the loops of a trace, report the one with the longest reach; ties go to the shorter cycle.
  3. Report it as (p, start, copies): start = n − reach is the index of the first call of the looping stretch, and copies = reach // p is the number of full copies in it. Return None for a trace with no loop.

Return one result per trace, in order. In this instance r is {{r}} in every check.
sections.constraints: Four traces of 60 000 calls in the timing check, each ending in one short loop that covers the last 60 to 70 percent of the trace, with a few stumbles early in the loop. Measuring every cycle length's reach call by call is O(n) per length and O(n²) per trace, and so is skipping the lengths that fail early, because every multiple of the loop's length is also a loop that reaches back to the start of the stretch. Something close to O(n) per trace is expected.
sections.assumptions: Traces, call ids, r and the cap are hypothetical; this definition of a loop is this exercise's rule, so check current docs for how any real tool reports or limits repeated calls. Equal ids mean equal calls; deciding that two calls are "the same" happened before this function. r ≥ 2.
sections.criteria: The reach defined from the end of the trace and computed correctly, including stretches that begin part way through a cycle; loops only with at least r full copies; the longest reach chosen with ties to the shorter cycle, not the shortest repeating cycle; None for traces with no loop, empty traces and traces shorter than r; at Very Hard, the cap applied to the cycle length, not to the reach; an O(n) method (Z-function or an equivalent) with a clear explanation of why per-length scanning is quadratic on long loops; sensible answers on streaming detection, fuzzy equality of calls and what to store.

clarifications.q: Why not report the shortest cycle that repeats r times?
clarifications.a: Because a trace like search, open, open, search, open, open, search, open, open ends in "open, open": a one-call cycle that repeats twice. The loop that wasted the calls is three calls long and covers the whole trace. The longest reach is the loop to report.

clarifications.q: Does the looping stretch have to begin at the start of a cycle?
clarifications.a: No. It can begin part way through one; start is its first call, and copies counts only full copies.

clarifications.q: A cycle and its double reach equally far. Which do I report?
clarifications.a: The shorter one.

clarifications.q: The model looped for a while and then made one different call.
clarifications.a: That loop is over. A trace is judged only by the calls that end it: unless some cycle repeats at least r times up to and including the last call, return None.

clarifications.q: What about an empty trace, or one shorter than r?
clarifications.a: No cycle length qualifies, so None.

hints: Read the trace backwards. "The calls at the end that repeat with period p" becomes "how long the reversed trace agrees with itself shifted by p".
For the reversed trace s, let z[p] be the length of the longest common prefix of s and s[p:]. Then the reach of p is p + z[p], capped at n.
The Z-function computes z for every shift in O(n), reusing the rightmost window [left, right) already known to match the start of s. Then one pass over p picks the loop.
followups: Prove that a multiple of a loop's cycle length reaches exactly as far as the loop itself. Does skipping multiples make the call-by-call approach fast enough on every trace?
The trace now streams in. Flag the loop at the call that completes the r-th copy. What changes, and what would you keep per response?
The model rephrases its query slightly on every lap, so the calls are not exactly equal. How would you decide that two calls are the same, and where in the pipeline should that rule live?
Across all responses in a day, the console should show each team its wasted calls by tool. What would you store per response, and what would you never store?

rules.ask: What does z[p] mean for the reversed trace, and why is the reach of p equal to p + z[p]?
The prefix function gives the borders of each prefix. How would you get the reach of every cycle length from it, and is it still one pass?
Your check stops early when a length cannot reach r copies. How many calls does it walk for a length that can, on a 40 000-call loop of 3 calls, and how many such lengths are there?
Take search, open, open repeated three times with r = 2. Which cycle does your code report, and is that the loop?
How do you compare two blocks of calls with hashes, and how do you make sure a collision never reports a loop that is not there?

templates.title: Verbatim overlap with a cited source — the longest run of words a response shares with what it cites
templates.subtopic: binary search on the length + rolling hash with verification (or a suffix automaton)

sections.scenario: A response that cites a web page or a public post may quote it. Teams using the search tools want to know how much of a response repeats a cited source word for word, so that quotes can be shown as quotes and answers that copy long passages instead of summarising them can be found. Before this step, the citation pipeline has turned both texts into integer word ids; this exercise uses synthetic tokens, and no text is involved. For each citation it reports the longest run of consecutive words the response shares with the source, and where that run is in each.
sections.problem: Implement verbatim_overlap(response, sources). response is a list of integer word ids; sources lists the sources the response cites, in citation order, each a list of word ids. For each source, return (length, i, j): the largest length such that response[i:i + length] == source[j:j + length] for some i and j, and among runs of that length the smallest i, then the smallest j. Return (0, -1, -1) for a source that shares no word with the response, including an empty source. {{level_rule}} Return one tuple per source, in order.
sections.constraints: A 10 000-word response and 36 000 words of sources in the timing check. The longest-common-substring table has 360 million cells: too slow in Python even when it keeps only two rows, and slow even when each diagonal is compared in C. Something close to O((n + m) log n) is expected. The answer must be exact: a hash may find candidates, but a hash collision must never change the result.
sections.assumptions: Responses, sources and word ids are hypothetical; tokenisation happened earlier and equal ids are equal words. This overlap measure is this exercise's rule; check current docs for how any real product reports quotes or citations. Nothing here stores or inspects the text of a response or a source.
sections.criteria: The longest shared run found exactly, with the tie rule (earliest in the response, then in the source) and (0, -1, -1) for no shared word or an empty source; runs that overlap themselves handled; at Very Hard, one answer per cited source in order; a method close to O((n + m) log n) (binary search with a verified rolling hash) or O(n + m) (suffix automaton), with a clear account of why the quadratic table is too slow; hash collisions that can never change the answer; sensible answers on reporting every quote, per-source precomputation and fuzzy quoting.

clarifications.q: Can the run overlap itself, for a word repeated many times?
clarifications.a: Yes. Positions in the response and in the source are independent: a response [7, 7, 7, 7] and a source [7, 7, 7] give (3, 0, 0).

clarifications.q: Two runs have the same length. Which one do I report?
clarifications.a: The one starting earliest in the response; if it occurs several times in the source, the earliest place in the source.

clarifications.q: May I compare hashes instead of words?
clarifications.a: To find candidates, yes. The reported run must be verified word by word, and a collision must not change the answer.

clarifications.q: Are sentence boundaries or punctuation special?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. A run is any sequence of consecutive word ids.

clarifications.q: Does a run of one word count?
clarifications.a: Yes, (1, i, j).

hints: If the response shares a run of length L with a source, it shares a run of every shorter length. So the length can be binary searched.
For one length L, hash every window of L words in the source with a rolling hash and keep the first position per hash. Then slide over the response from the left and look each window up.

Verify each hit by comparing the words. If a verification ever fails, decide that length by an exact method, so a collision can only cost time, never correctness. Scanning the response from the left and keeping the first source position gives the tie rule for free.
Another linear route: a suffix automaton of the source, with the response walked through it, keeping the earliest end positions.
followups: Report every run of at least k words, not only the longest, so the page can mark each quote. What changes in your method, and in its cost?
One popular source is cited by thousands of responses a day. What would you precompute for that source, and how long would you keep it?
The response quotes with small changes: one word replaced every few words. What measure would you use instead of an exact run, and what does it cost?
Compare binary search with hashing, a suffix automaton and a suffix array on memory, worst case and ease of getting the tie rule right.

rules.ask: How many cells does your table have for a 10 000-word response and 36 000 words of sources, and how long does that take in Python?
Two different windows can share a hash. Where does your code catch a collision, and what does it do then?
Why is "a shared run of length L exists" monotone in L, and how do you keep the earliest i and j at the final length?
Your structure gives the length. How do you recover the earliest i and j as well?
Keeping every window as a tuple costs how much memory at a length of 500 words, and how many times does the binary search do it?

templates.title: Debug the citation report for server-side tool calls
templates.subtopic: URL canonicalisation before deduplication, subdomain folding, web and post citations apart, denominators, UTC days

sections.scenario: Each day, teams that use the server-side search tools see a citation report for their own responses: how many responses ran, how many cited anything, how many distinct web pages and public posts they cited, and which sites. Teams have reported problems. A page cited once with a tracking parameter and once without counts as two citations. Every site under a two-label suffix such as .co.uk appears as one site called co.uk. Web citations are higher than the web pages in the responses, by exactly the number of post citations. The share of responses with a citation looks too high, and days on which no response cited anything are missing. A response at 22:00 in California on the 5th appears on the 5th, though it is already the 6th in UTC. The report code below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix citation_report(responses, suffixes) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Input. Each response is a dict {"id", "ts", "citations"}. ts is an ISO 8601 time with a UTC offset, such as 2026-10-05T22:00:00-07:00. Each citation is {"kind", "ref"}: a "web" citation's ref is a URL, and a "post" citation's ref is a public post's id.
  2. Day. A response belongs to the UTC date of its ts, as "YYYY-MM-DD".
  3. Canonical URL (this exercise's rule). The host is lowercased and a leading www. removed; the scheme is ignored, so http and https give the same page; the path keeps its case, with trailing slashes removed; the fragment is dropped; query parameters whose name starts with utm_ are removed and the others kept in their order. The canonical form is the host, then the path, then ? and the remaining parameters if any remain. Hosts carry no port or user info.
  4. Site. A web citation's site is the last two labels of its canonical host, or the last three when the last two labels, joined by a dot, are listed in suffixes (such as "co.uk").
  5. Deduplication. Within one response, web citations count once per canonical URL and post citations once per post id. A post citation is never a web citation and has no site.
  6. Output. {day: {"responses", "cited", "web", "posts", "domains"}}: every response that day, cited or not; the responses with at least one citation of either kind; distinct web citations summed over the responses; distinct post citations summed over the responses; and, per site, the number of responses that day citing it at least once. A day appears when it has at least one response.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. 50 000 responses in the timing check, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Responses, URLs (all on generic example domains), post ids and the suffix list are hypothetical; the canonical form and the site rule are this exercise's rules, so check current docs for how any real tool returns or groups citations. The report shows a team only its own responses. Nothing here inspects the text of a response, a page or a post.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its user-facing symptom; URLs canonicalised before deduplication, with the path's case kept and only utm_ parameters removed; the site fold that checks the last two labels against the suffix list; post citations counted apart and never given a site; responses without citations kept in the denominator and their days kept; days computed by converting to UTC; minimal fixes with a regression check per bug.

clarifications.q: Are http://example.com/a and https://www.example.com/a/ the same page?
clarifications.a: Yes, under this exercise's rule.

clarifications.q: Are /A and /a the same page?
clarifications.a: No. Paths keep their case.

clarifications.q: A response cites the same post twice.
clarifications.a: It counts once in that response. Another response citing it counts once more.

clarifications.q: Does a response with only post citations count as cited?
clarifications.a: Yes. "Cited" means at least one citation of either kind.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Write the same page five ways, with www., a tracking parameter, a fragment and a trailing slash, and follow them through the loop. Where does deduplication happen, and on what?
Call _domain("news.example.co.uk", ["co.uk"]) by hand.
Count the places where d["web"] goes up.
Which responses ever reach the counters?
What does ts[:10] give for 2026-10-05T22:00:00-07:00?
followups: The suffix list here has two entries. A real public suffix list has thousands of rules, with wildcards and exceptions. How would you obtain and version it, and what happens to old reports when it changes?
A site redirects /a to /b. Should both count as one citation? Where would that knowledge come from, and what would it cost?
The report for a past day must be reproducible a month later. What would you store with each day's numbers?
A team in UTC+9 wants the report in its own days. What changes, and what stays in UTC?

rules.ask: In which order do you canonicalise and deduplicate, and what does the other order count for a page cited with a tracking parameter?
What does your fold give for example.co.uk itself, with three labels, and for shop.example.com.au?
Which date does your code give for 22:00 at −07:00 on the 5th, and why is that the 6th?
Which responses are in your denominator, and where does a day with no citations at all appear?
Can a post citation ever have a site? What would your fix do if a post id looked like a URL?

templates.title: Public-post ingestion pipeline — creates, edits and deletions in, a searchable index out, and the lag measured stage by stage
templates.subtopic: per-key ordering, deletions that overtake creates, versioned enrichment, replay, stage-by-stage lag

2: 5,000 events a second on average and 40,000 at peaks
3: 20,000 events a second on average and 150,000 at peaks
50,000 events a second on average and 300,000 at peaks

sections.scenario: A model API offers a server-side tool that searches recent public posts, so that a response can find and cite them. Posts arrive as a stream of events with a given schema: a create (post id, an opaque author key, creation time, text as synthetic tokens, optional reply, quote and repost references), later edits that replace the text, and deletions. The stream carries about {{posts_per_second}}. Before a post can be found it passes several stages: schema validation, a language label from a classifier you are given (with its version), tokenisation and an embedding from a model you are given (with its version), and the index write. In this exercise's rules (check current docs), a post should be searchable within {{searchable_target}} of its creation, and a deleted post must leave search within {{delete_target}} of the deletion event, wherever it is in the pipeline.
sections.problem: Design the ingestion pipeline. Cover how events are partitioned and ordered (per post), what happens when a deletion or an edit arrives before the create it refers to, how duplicates from at-least-once delivery are absorbed, how each stage records its work, how edits replace earlier versions in the index, how a deletion reaches every stage, cache and index replica in time and is never undone by a delayed create or edit, how you re-run the last {{replay_days}} days when the classifier or embedding version changes, and how you measure the lag from creation to searchable, stage by stage, so that a slow stage can be found within minutes.
sections.constraints: Events arrive at least once and can be out of order across posts and, rarely, within a post. A deletion is final: no later stage may make that post searchable again. The searchable and deletion targets above are measured per post, and the report must show their 50th and 95th percentiles per hour, per stage and per language label. A replay must not change the lag numbers of the hours it re-processes, and must not resurrect deleted posts. Peaks are several times the average.
sections.assumptions: Volumes and targets are hypothetical. The schema, the language classifier and the embedding model are given; nothing here is about moderating content, and text is synthetic tokens. Authors appear only as opaque keys and only in aggregate. Ranking of search results is a scoring function you are given and is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Per-post ordering with versions; deletions that overtake creates handled with durable tombstones; idempotent stages under at-least-once delivery; edits replacing earlier versions; deletions propagated to every stage, cache and replica within the target and never undone; replays on a separate lane that preserve lag numbers and deletions; lag stamped per stage and reported as percentiles per hour, stage and language; bounded copies of text; sensible handling of peaks without dropping deletions.

clarifications.q: Can a deletion really arrive before its create?
clarifications.a: Yes, rarely, when the create was delayed upstream. The post must never become searchable.

clarifications.q: Is an edit a new post?
clarifications.a: No. It is a new version of the same post id; the index keeps only the latest version, and lag is measured for each version from the edit time.

clarifications.q: Where does "searchable" begin?
clarifications.a: When a query against the serving index can return the post, not when the index write was acknowledged by one replica.

clarifications.q: May we drop events at peaks?
clarifications.a: Never deletions. You may say how creates degrade (delayed, not lost) and what the report shows meanwhile.

clarifications.q: Do we keep the text after indexing?
clarifications.a: Only what the index needs, for as long as the post is searchable and not deleted; say how the copies in the pipeline are bounded.

hints: Partition by post id so that every event of a post goes through the same ordered lane; give each event a sequence or version per post.
Keep a small per-post state (latest version, deleted flag) that every stage consults; a deletion writes a tombstone that outlives the post's retention so a late create can be recognised and dropped.
Stamp each event with the time it entered and left every stage; compute percentiles from those stamps with event-time windows, and keep replays in a separate lane with their own stamps.
followups: The classifier version changes. Walk through the {{replay_days}}-day replay: what is re-run, what stays searchable meanwhile, and how do the two versions coexist?
One stage is slow for an hour. Show the report that tells you which stage, and what the searchable lag looks like for posts created in that hour.
Deletions spike to ten times their usual rate. How do you keep the deletion target without starving creates?
A downstream team wants every version of every post for research. What would you say, and what would you offer instead?

rules.ask: You partition by post id. What happens to a very active post, and to ordering when the partition count changes?
How long does a tombstone live, and what happens if a delayed create arrives after it has expired?
Which key makes a duplicate edit harmless at the index write, and what if two edits carry the same version?
How do you compute an hourly p95 of searchable lag when some posts of that hour are still in the pipeline?
A deletion reached the index but a cached result still holds the post. How does your design meet the deletion target there?

templates.title: Server-side tool call logging — every search a response ran, its results and citations, latency per tool, failures, and calls billed by rule
templates.subtopic: per-call records, call ids across retries, latency histograms per tool, billing derived from logs and reconciled

billing_rule: each tool call that completed is billed once, and failed calls are not billed
each tool call that returned at least one result is billed once, and failed or empty calls are not billed

sections.scenario: A response that uses server-side tools may run up to {{max_calls}} tool calls: web searches, searches over public posts, opening a result. About {{responses_per_day}} such responses run a day, across several regions. Teams want to see, for their own usage, each search their responses ran, the results and citations that came back, how long each tool took and which calls failed. Billing needs the number of billable calls per team and day under this exercise's rule (check current docs): {{billing_rule}}. Inside the platform, a call can be retried after a timeout, and a streaming response can be cancelled while a call is still running.
sections.problem: Design the logging of server-side tool calls and the tables built from it. Cover the call record and its identifiers (response, call sequence, attempts), what is logged about the query, results and citations, how retries and cancellations are represented, how latency is recorded per tool and per stage of a call and reported as percentiles, how failures are classified, how billable calls are derived and reconciled with the usage the invoice shows, retention for {{log_retention_days}} days, and what a team can see versus what only aggregate reporting sees.
sections.constraints: Every call is logged exactly once in the billing tables, however many internal attempts it took and however many times a log line is delivered. Billing must be reproducible for any past day. Latency is reported per tool as percentiles per hour, never as an average alone. Queries can contain a user's words, so the log must minimise and protect them; results and citations are logged as references, not page or post contents. Logs from all regions must reconcile with the per-team usage totals daily.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the call budget, the billing rule and retention are hypothetical and this exercise's rules; check current docs for how tool calls are actually billed. Tools, their stages and their failure kinds are generic. Teams appear only as their own usage to themselves and in aggregate otherwise.
sections.criteria: A call record keyed by response and sequence with attempts beneath it; retries, timeouts and cancellations represented explicitly; results and citations logged as references; latency as stage durations with percentile reporting from mergeable histograms per tool and hour; failure classes; billable calls derived from final states by the stated rule, deduplicated on the call id, reproducible and reconciled daily with usage; query data minimised with stated access and retention; team views limited to the team's own usage.

clarifications.q: A web search timed out and was retried internally, and the retry succeeded. How many billable calls?
clarifications.a: One. The attempts are logged, but the call the model asked for is billed once by the rule.

clarifications.q: The response was cancelled while a call was running.
clarifications.a: Log the call as cancelled with what is known; whether it is billable follows from the rule (it did not complete).

clarifications.q: May we log the full query text?
clarifications.a: Decide and justify. The requirement is to support a team's own view and aggregate reporting with the least data; say what you keep, for how long, and who can read it.

clarifications.q: Are results the same as citations?
clarifications.a: No. Results are what the tool returned to the model; citations are the results the response cited. Log both, as references.

clarifications.q: Can billing come from a separate meter?
clarifications.a: It can, but it must reconcile with the logs every day, and differences must be explainable per call.

hints: Give each call an id derived from the response id and the call's sequence number, and each attempt an attempt number under it; billing keys on the call id.
Write latency as stage durations on the attempt (queue, search, fetch) and the total on the call; percentiles come from histograms per tool and hour, which merge across regions.
Derive billable calls from final call states with the stated rule, deduplicated on the call id, and reconcile daily with the usage totals per team.
followups: Billable calls for one team doubled overnight while its responses did not. List the logging and pipeline causes you would check before believing it.
The billing rule changes next quarter. How do you apply the new rule from a date without changing past invoices, and how do you show both?
A team asks why one response was slow. What can you show from the logs, and what can you not show?
At {{responses_per_day}} responses a day, where does the cost of these logs go, and what would you sample, aggregate or drop first without touching billing?

rules.ask: Where does the attempt number live, and which key keeps a retried call from being billed twice?
The average latency did not move but users complain. Which number would have shown the problem, and how do you compute it across regions?
Which of your tables can be sampled and which can never be, given that billing comes from them?
Who can read that field, how long is it kept, and could a hash or a team-only view answer the same question?
Your daily totals differ from the usage meter by 0.3 percent. How do you find the calls that explain it?

templates.title: Spend tiers as data — a spend ledger, versioned thresholds, tier changes and the per-model limits in force for a request
templates.subtopic: ledger-derived state, versioned thresholds without retroactive demotion, effective-dated limit tables, as-of reconstruction

sections.scenario: A model API limits each team, per model, in requests per second and tokens per minute. In this exercise (check current docs for the real rules) the limits come from the team's spend tier: there are {{tiers}} tiers, and a team moves up when its cumulative spend reaches the next tier's threshold. The platform offers {{models}} models, some behind aliases, each with its own limits per tier. About {{teams}} teams are active, and the billing side produces spend events at about {{spend_events}}: usage charges, refunds, chargebacks and usage paid by promotional credits. Thresholds are revised from time to time, models launch and retire, and limits per model and tier change. Developers and support ask the same questions every day: which tier was this team in at 14:05 last Tuesday, which limits applied to its request to this model, why — and how far is it from the next tier?
sections.problem: Design the data model for spend tiers and the limits they grant. Cover the spend ledger and which entries count as spend; cumulative spend per team; threshold versions; tier changes as dated events with their cause; per-model limits for each tier as versioned data, including aliases; and a derived view that returns the limits in force for (team, model or alias, instant). Show how a request's limits are reconstructed after the fact, including when a spend event arrived late or a threshold version changed in between.
sections.constraints: Money is stored in integer cents (usage may be metered in smaller integer units and rounded when charged). In this exercise's rules: cumulative spend is lifetime spend from paid usage and refunds; usage paid by promotional credits never counts. A tier, once reached, is never lowered automatically; only a recorded manual decision with a reason lowers it. A new threshold version never demotes anyone: when thresholds rise, teams keep the tier they have; when they fall, teams that now qualify move up when the version takes effect. A tier change must reach request handling within minutes of the spend event that caused it. Limits exist per (model, tier); a model with no limits row for a tier is not offered to that tier, and a missing row is never read as zero or as unlimited. Nothing is overwritten.
sections.assumptions: Team counts, tier counts, model counts, spend volumes and every threshold and limit are hypothetical. Per-team limit overrides and project-level caps are out of scope; the limiting algorithm itself is out of scope — you design the data it reads.
sections.criteria: Ledger entries as immutable facts with a stated rule for what counts; cumulative spend and tier history derived, with each tier interval tied to its cause; threshold versions applied from their effective time without retroactive demotion; limits per (model, tier) as versioned rows with aliases resolved as of the request; a missing limits row treated as "not offered", never zero; an as-of query that reconstructs any past request's limits; an incremental path for crossings within minutes; the incidents explained by the model and fixed without rewriting history.

clarifications.q: Is cumulative spend lifetime, or per month?
clarifications.a: Lifetime since the team was created, in this exercise. Check current docs for how the real product counts it.

clarifications.q: When does a charge count — when usage happens or when it is paid?
clarifications.a: When it is charged to the team. A chargeback later is a negative ledger entry; say what it does to the tier under the rules above.

clarifications.q: Can one payment cross several thresholds?
clarifications.a: Yes. Record one change per tier crossed, or one change to the highest tier — state which, and what the history shows.

clarifications.q: Are limits per model or per model family?
clarifications.a: Per model. A request may name an alias, and an alias can be moved to a newer model with different limits.

clarifications.q: How long must history be answerable?
clarifications.a: Two years, for support and for billing disputes.

hints: Keep facts (ledger entries, threshold versions, limit versions, alias moves) apart from derived state (cumulative spend, tier history, limits in force).
A team's tier history is a set of intervals [from, to) per team, each pointing at the event that opened it: a spend crossing, a threshold version, or a manual decision.
"Limits in force at t" is three as-of lookups: the alias's target at t, the team's tier interval containing t, and the limits version for (model, tier) in force at t.
followups: Write the query, or pseudocode, that returns the requests-per-second and tokens-per-minute limits for team T, alias A, at instant t, and the rows that justify them.
A refund arrives two days late for the payment that pushed a team over a threshold. Which rows change, and does the team's tier history change under this exercise's rules?
A new threshold version raises the threshold of the second-highest of the {{tiers}} tiers. Which teams move, which rows are written, and what does a team that was one dollar short see the next day?
A model launches with limits for only some of the {{tiers}} tiers. How does your model keep it from teams in the other tiers, and what check finds the gap before launch?
At {{spend_events}}, how do you keep cumulative spend and tier crossings current within minutes without summing a team's ledger on every request?

rules.ask: Support asks which tier a team was in when its request was rejected last Tuesday at 14:05. With the tier stored as a column on the team, how do you answer?
A refund for last month arrives today. Does your cumulative spend rewrite last month's tier history, and should it under this exercise's rules?
A new model has no limits row for the lowest tier. What does your fallback give a team in that tier, and is that the behaviour you want?
A team crosses a threshold. How long until every request handler sees the new limits, and what does a request in between get?
An alias moves to a newer model with lower limits in one tier. Which limits apply to a request that named the alias one second before the move, and how does your model show it?

incidents: After a threshold version raised the thresholds, a nightly job recomputed every team's tier from the new version and moved 3% of teams down one of the {{tiers}} tiers; their requests were rejected the next morning, against the rule that a new version never demotes anyone.

A model launched with limits for every tier but the lowest. The lookup defaulted the missing row to zero, and every request from lowest-tier teams to that model was rejected for most of a day with a message that pointed at the team's usage.

A chargeback reversed the payment that had moved a team up a tier. By rule the tier stayed, but finance asked for it to be reviewed, and the model had no place to record a manual decision, its reason or who made it.

templates.title: Public posts as retrieval documents — versions, edits, deletions, reposts and quotes, and the exact version a request retrieved
templates.subtopic: entity versus version, tombstones that outlive content, derived documents with dependencies, retrieval provenance without copies

sections.scenario: A model API offers a server-side tool that searches recent public posts, so a response can cite them. Posts arrive with a given schema: a post id, an opaque author key, a creation time, text (synthetic tokens in this exercise), a language label from a classifier you are given (with its version), and optional reply_to, quote_of and repost_of references; edits and deletions arrive later as events. About {{posts_per_day}} posts arrive a day. In this exercise's rules (check current docs): an author can edit a post within {{edit_window_minutes}} minutes of posting, and each edit makes a new version; a deleted post must leave retrieval within {{delete_sla}}; and the index holds the last {{index_days}} days. Teams using the tool ask which version of a post their response retrieved and cited.
sections.problem: Design the data model for public posts as retrieval documents. Cover post identity and versions; deletion as a tombstone; reposts and quotes; language labels with the classifier version that produced them; the documents the index holds (what a quote's document contains, and whether reposts get documents at all); and a retrieval record that says exactly which post version each request retrieved and cited, without keeping deleted content anywhere.
sections.constraints: No post content beyond what the schema gives. Authors appear only as opaque keys and only in aggregate; nothing in the model builds a profile of an author. A deletion removes the post's text from every copy (versions, index documents, caches, any document that embedded it) within {{delete_sla}}, and the tombstone keeps only ids and times. A repost has no text of its own. Retrieval records keep ids and version numbers, never text. Ordering of results is a scoring function you are given and is out of scope.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, windows, the deletion target and retention are hypothetical. The classifier, the embedding model and the scoring function are given to you as versioned black boxes. The ingestion pipeline itself is out of scope; you design what it writes.
sections.criteria: Post, version and document kept as separate keyed entities; edits as versions within the edit window; deletion as a tombstone that removes text from every copy within the target, with dependencies recorded so quotes are rebuilt; reposts resolved to their original rather than indexed as copies; labels stored with their classifier version; retrieval records with post id, version and index generation and no text; authors as opaque keys used only in aggregate; sizing tied to {{posts_per_day}} and {{index_days}} days; the incidents traced to missing versions, missing dependencies or incomplete deletion.

clarifications.q: Does an edit get a new post id?
clarifications.a: No. Same post id, a new version number. An earlier response may have retrieved the earlier version.

clarifications.q: Should reposts be searchable?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say what a search that matches an original returns when ten thousand reposts of it exist.

clarifications.q: Can a deleted post come back?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise.

clarifications.q: Can the language label change?
clarifications.a: Yes. The classifier is re-run when it is upgraded, and some labels change.

clarifications.q: Months later, must we show the text a response cited?
clarifications.a: Only while the post exists and within the index's retention; after a deletion only ids remain.

hints: Separate three things: the post (identity and status), its versions (text and times), and index documents (what the search reads), each with its own key.
A quote's document depends on the quoted post. Record that dependency so a deletion or edit can find every document to rebuild.
Log retrieval by (post id, version, index generation or time), not by copying what was shown.
followups: List the rows that exist after a post is created, edited once, quoted by another post, reposted twice, and then deleted.
A response retrieves version 1 of a post; an edit lands 20 seconds later. What does the team's citation link show, and what does your retrieval record say?
A post is reposted 50 000 times in an hour. How does your document model keep a search from returning many copies of the same text?
The language classifier is upgraded and relabels 8% of posts. How do the label rows, the index and past retrieval records reflect it?
Estimate rows and bytes a day for versions, documents and retrieval records at {{posts_per_day}}, and how {{index_days}} days of retention bound them.

rules.ask: Your row is flagged deleted, but its text is still in it. Where else does that text live, and how do you show it is gone from all of them within {{delete_sla}}?
A team asks which words their response cited yesterday, and the post was edited since. What does your model return?
The quoted post is deleted. Which documents still contain its text, and how do you find them all?
Authors appear here only in aggregate. Which questions need the author key at all, and what stops this model from becoming a profile of a person?
An edit changes three tokens. Do you re-embed, and what does a search between the edit and the new embedding return?

incidents: A post deleted at 10:00 was cited in a response at 10:40, far past the {{delete_sla}} rule: the deletion removed the latest version's document, but a document for an earlier version was still in the index.
After an edit, a team's console showed the edited text beside a citation made before the edit; the retrieval record kept only the post id, so nobody could say which version had been cited.
A quote post's document still carried the text of a quoted post deleted the day before, because quote documents were built once at ingest and nothing recorded which documents depended on which post.

templates.title: Tool calls and citations as data — the searches a response ran, the results returned, and citations attached to spans
templates.subtopic: per-call results versus global sources, span offsets in a stated unit, many-to-many citations, canonical URLs, retention

sections.scenario: A model API can run server-side tools inside a response: a web search and a search over public posts. In this exercise the model may run {{calls_per_response}} tool calls in one response; each call returns up to {{results_per_call}} results ordered by a scoring function you are given; and the final response attaches citations to spans of its text, each pointing at a result. About {{responses_per_day}} responses a day use tools. A team's console shows, per response, the searches run, what came back and which sources were cited; analysts ask how often a source or domain is cited across responses; and a team's tool data is kept {{retention_days}} days (this exercise's rule; check current docs).
sections.problem: Design the data model: responses; tool calls (tool, parameters, status, position in the response); results per call (rank, source); sources (a web page by canonical URL and domain, or a public post by id and version); and citations (a span of the response text and the result it cites). Say which unit span offsets use, how a source returned by two calls stays one source, how a streamed response's citations are attached, and how the data expires per team.
sections.constraints: Span offsets use one stated unit over the final response text; clients that count differently convert at the edge. A citation must reference a result returned in the same response; a citation the model produced for something no call returned is kept and flagged, never silently dropped. A post source records the post's version; a deleted post keeps only its id and version here. Web page content is not stored: only the canonical URL, domain, title hash and fetch time. A tool call's parameters can contain the team's own text and are treated as the team's data, deleted with it.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, limits and retention are hypothetical. Billing of tool calls and per-tool latency monitoring are out of scope here. The scoring function, the canonicalisation rules and the post schema are given; your model must record which version of each it used.
sections.criteria: Responses, calls, results, sources and citations as separate tables with clear keys; citations referencing results (not only sources); a stated offset unit with conversion at the edges; canonical URLs with a versioned rule; post sources with version and tombstone behaviour; unreturned citations flagged; parameters treated as the team's data with per-team expiry; partitioning sized to {{responses_per_day}}; the incidents traced to offset units, join grain and copies that deletions did not reach.

clarifications.q: Can one span cite several sources?
clarifications.a: Yes, and one source can be cited by several spans.

clarifications.q: Is the response streamed?
clarifications.a: Yes. In this exercise citations arrive at the end, with offsets into the final text.

clarifications.q: Two calls return the same URL. One source or two?
clarifications.a: One source, two results. Say how URLs are canonicalised and where the rule lives.

clarifications.q: Are failed tool calls kept?
clarifications.a: Yes, with their status; a response may continue without them.

clarifications.q: Does a citation keep the snippet that was shown?
clarifications.a: Not the text: a hash and offsets are enough for this exercise.

hints: Results belong to a call; sources are shared; citations point at results, which keeps "which call found it" answerable.
Choose one offset unit (for example Unicode code points of the final text), store it, and name it in the schema.
Canonicalisation is a versioned rule; store the raw URL and the canonical one, with the rule version.
followups: Draw the rows for one response that ran two searches, got 15 results, and cited four spans, two of them the same URL found by both searches.
A client renders text in UTF-16. How do you convert offsets, and how would you test the conversion?
Write the query: per team and day, the share of tool-using responses with at least one citation, and the most-cited domains, counting a response once per domain.
A post cited in a response is deleted. What does the console show afterwards, and which rows change?
At {{responses_per_day}}, which tables are append-only facts, how would you partition them, and how do you expire a team's rows after {{retention_days}} days?

rules.ask: Analysts ask for last week's most-cited domains. How do they query citations kept in one JSON document per response at {{responses_per_day}} a day?
Which unit are your offsets in, and what happens to a citation in a response containing emoji when a client counts in a different unit?
The same article arrives as http and https, with tracking parameters and a trailing slash. Is that one source or four, and where is the rule kept?
A citation points straight at a source. Two calls returned that source; how do you tell which result the model used?

incidents: After a client library release, citations in responses containing non-ASCII text highlighted the wrong words: the server counted UTF-8 bytes and the library counted UTF-16 code units.

A "citations per response" chart doubled after a release: each citation was joined to every result with the same URL, and with {{calls_per_response}} calls per response the same URL often came back twice.
Citations to deleted posts kept showing the post's text in team consoles for weeks, from a cache keyed by post id that the deletion never reached.

templates.title: Regional endpoints as data — models per region, versioned price multipliers, residency settings, and the region that served each request
templates.subtopic: effective-dated availability and multipliers, settings history, decisions recorded on the fact, exact money, invoice reconciliation

sections.scenario: A model API offers a global endpoint and regional endpoints in {{regions}} regions. In this exercise (check current docs for the real rules): a request served through a regional endpoint is billed at the model's base price times that region's price multiplier, and multipliers change at announced times; not every one of the {{models}} models is offered in every region; and a team can set a residency setting that pins its requests to one region or a set of regions. About {{pinned_share}} of teams use one. The platform serves about {{requests_per_day}} requests a day. Teams ask why a request cost what it did and where it was served; finance needs every invoice line to match the console.
sections.problem: Design the data model: regions and their endpoints; model availability per region over time; price multiplier versions; base price versions per model; each team's residency setting history; and a request fact that records the endpoint called, the region that served it, the model version, the multiplier version and base price version applied, and the exact cost. Then show how a team's monthly cost per region is reproduced from the facts and checked against the invoice.
sections.constraints: Money and multipliers are exact (integer micro-cents and decimal multipliers, or another exact scheme you state). In this exercise the multiplier and base price in force at the time a request is received apply, whenever it finishes. A pinned team's request is never served outside its allowed regions; if that ever happens, the fact must show it. A pinned team calling a model not offered in its region gets an explicit error, never a silent reroute. History is never overwritten. Request content stays in the region that served it; only billing fields (counts, tokens, cost, versions) are aggregated across regions.
sections.assumptions: Region counts, model counts, volumes, prices and multipliers are hypothetical. The global endpoint bills at base price in this exercise. Routing and failover machinery is out of scope; you design the data it reads and writes.
sections.criteria: Regions, endpoints, availability, multipliers, base prices and residency settings as effective-dated rows; the request fact recording endpoint called, region served, setting version and every price version applied; exact money with a stated rounding point; received time as the pricing instant, applied the same way in facts and invoices; withdrawals with end dates and explicit errors; content kept in region with only billing fields aggregated; an invoice reproducible from facts; the incidents explained by missing columns or inconsistent time rules.

clarifications.q: A multiplier changes at 00:00 UTC. Which applies to a request received at 23:59:59 that finishes at 00:00:05?
clarifications.a: The one in force when it was received, in this exercise.

clarifications.q: Can a team change its residency setting?
clarifications.a: Yes, effective from when it is saved; requests already received keep the setting they started with.

clarifications.q: Is the base price the same in every region?
clarifications.a: Yes; base prices are versioned separately from multipliers.

clarifications.q: Can a model be withdrawn from a region?
clarifications.a: Yes, with an announced end date; pinned teams must be told before it happens.

clarifications.q: Does the invoice show regions?
clarifications.a: Yes: one line per model, region and price version within the month.

hints: Keep three effective-dated things apart: model availability per region, multipliers, and residency settings.
Put the decisions on the fact (versions applied, region served, setting version), so billing never re-derives them from tables that changed since.
The endpoint a team called and the region that served the request are different columns.
followups: Write the query that recomputes one team's monthly cost per region and price version from request facts and compares it to its invoice lines.

A multiplier change announced for the 1st was entered with the 2nd as its effective date and found on the 10th. How do you correct invoices already issued, and what do the version rows look like afterwards?
A model is withdrawn from one region. Which rows change, and what do pinned teams see before and after the end date?
Across {{regions}} regions, how do you keep request facts in region and still produce one global usage console and one invoice per team?

rules.ask: A multiplier of 1.1 on a price of a fraction of a cent per thousand tokens, summed over {{requests_per_day}} requests: what type keeps the invoice equal to the console?
A team changed its residency setting last week. From your model, which regions was it pinned to when last Monday's request was served?
The multiplier changed mid-month. Does looking it up at invoice time give the same answer as the price recorded at request time, and which one does the team expect?
The pinned region is unavailable. What does your model record for a request the policy refused, and for one that was served elsewhere by mistake?

incidents: A multiplier change at 00:00 UTC was applied by received time in the request facts but by completion time in the invoice job; one region's monthly invoice line differed from the console for long-running requests that straddled midnight.

A team pinned to one region saw requests in its console marked as served in another during an incident. The facts recorded only the endpoint called, so nobody could tell the team which requests had been served outside its region.

A model withdrawn from one of the {{regions}} regions kept appearing as available, because availability rows had no end dates; pinned teams got generic errors instead of a clear "not offered in this region".

templates.title: Spend tier reached — the first day each threshold was met, and rate-limit rejections in the week either side
templates.subtopic: running sums per day, effective-dated thresholds, first-crossing dates, date windows on timestamps, incomplete windows as NULL

sections.scenario: A model API limits each team, per model, in requests per second and tokens per minute, and the limits rise with the team's spend tier: a team reaches a tier when its cumulative spend reaches the tier's threshold (this exercise's tiers and thresholds; check current docs for the real ones). Developer relations want to know whether upgrades relieve throttling. For every team and every tier it reached in the sample, they want the day it reached the tier and the team's rate-limit rejections in the week before and the week after. The sample covers {{first_day}} to {{last_day}}, {{team_count}} teams and {{tier_count}} tiers.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns team_id, tier, reached_on, rejected_7d_before, rejected_7d_after, one row per team and tier reached, ordered by team_id, tier.

  • A team's cumulative spend at the end of a UTC day D is the sum of amount_cents over its spend_events of kind charge or refund with occurred_at on or before D (refund amounts are negative). Rows of kind promotional_credit are usage paid by free credits and never count. {{kinds_rule}} All of each team's spend falls inside the sample.
  • Tier k's threshold on day D is the min_spend_cents of the tier_thresholds row for tier k with effective_from <= D and (effective_to IS NULL or D < effective_to). {{threshold_rule}}
  • A team reaches tier k on the first day of the sample whose end-of-day cumulative spend is at least that day's threshold for k.
