Spend that crosses a threshold during a day and is refunded the same day does not reach it. A tier is reached once: dipping below it later and crossing again adds nothing. Several tiers can be reached on the same day.
  • rejected_7d_before is the number of request_errors rows for the team with status_code 429 and requested_at on one of the 7 UTC days reached_on − 7 through reached_on − 1; rejected_7d_after likewise for reached_on + 1 through reached_on + 7. The day the tier was reached is in neither. A window with no such rows is 0. A window that does not lie wholly inside the sample ({{first_day}} to {{last_day}}) is NULL. {{window_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). occurred_at and requested_at are TIMESTAMPTZ, and the session time zone is UTC. The sample has {{spend_rows}} spend events and {{error_rows}} error rows; in production there are hundreds of thousands of teams and a year of history.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical teams, amounts, thresholds, models and errors. model and limit_hit are context only. The comparison is a simple before and after, not a causal estimate: a team's own traffic changes around an upgrade too.
sections.criteria: Counted spend netted per UTC day with refunds and without promotional credits; a running total per team by day; thresholds joined as of each day; the first qualifying day per team and tier, once; windows on whole UTC days that exclude the reached day; only 429s counted; NULL for windows that leave the sample; deterministic order; can discuss confounders, late spend, incremental crossings and splitting by limit type.

clarifications.q: Is spend checked after every charge, or once a day?
clarifications.a: Once per UTC day, at the end of the day.

clarifications.q: A refund takes a team back below a tier it reached. Does it lose the tier here?
clarifications.a: No. This report gives the first day the tier was reached, once.

clarifications.q: Do 400, 500 and 503 rows count as rejections?
clarifications.a: No. Only 429 is a rate-limit rejection.

clarifications.q: Can a team reach a tier on a day it spent nothing?
clarifications.a: Apply the rules as written: each day uses the threshold in force on that day.

clarifications.q: What if only part of a window is inside the sample?
clarifications.a: That window's count is NULL, not a partial count.

hints: Net the counted spend per team and UTC day, then take a running SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id ORDER BY day).
Join each team-day to the threshold rows in force that day, keep the rows where cumulative spend is at least the threshold, and take MIN(day) per team and tier.
Count the 429s by requested_at::date between two dates (or with half-open timestamp bounds), and wrap each count in a CASE that returns NULL for a window that runs off the sample.
If a threshold can change on a day a team spent nothing, a running total over spend days only never looks at that day; a calendar (generate_series) per team does.
followups: Rejections fall after most upgrades. What else changes for a team around an upgrade that could explain it, and what would you compare against?
Spend events can arrive up to two days late. How does that change reached_on, and how would you keep a published report stable?
At production scale, what would you store per team so that a new crossing is found without rescanning the ledger, and what forces a recompute?

Split the rejections by limit_hit. If requests-per-second rejections fall after an upgrade and tokens-per-minute rejections do not, what does that suggest about the tier's limits or the team's traffic?

rules.ask: LAG finds the days spend crossed a threshold. A team dips below a tier and crosses again; how many rows does your query return for that tier, and which date?
requested_at is a timestamp. Which of the seventh day's rejections does requested_at <= reached_on + 7 keep?
Which rows are you counting? Is every failed request a rate-limit rejection?
Is your running total per event or per day? A charge that crossed a threshold at 09:00 was refunded at 17:00; does your query say the team reached the tier?
How many rows does your calendar produce for a few hundred thousand teams over a year, and could you check only the days with spend plus the days a threshold version starts?

incidents: After a threshold version lowered one tier's threshold, the tier report missed every team that qualified on the day the version took effect: the job evaluated only teams with spend events that day.
A dashboard built on this report counted all 4xx and 5xx responses as throttling, so a one-day outage looked like a spike in rejections just before many upgrades.

templates.title: Rate limiting by spend tier — requests per second and tokens per minute, enforced across regions
templates.subtopic: per-model limits by tier, token reservations, regional shares, honest retry hints

sections.scenario: {{teams}} teams call a model API through regional endpoints in {{regions}} regions, at up to {{peak_rps}} requests a second across the platform at peak. Each team has, for each model, a limit on requests per second and a limit on tokens per minute. Both limits depend on the team's spend tier, which rises as the team's cumulative spend crosses published thresholds. In this exercise a team's limit for a model applies to all regions combined, and the tokens counted are input plus output tokens (this exercise's rule; check current docs). When a request would exceed a limit, the API answers with HTTP 429. Teams that pay and cross a threshold expect their new limits within {{upgrade_minutes}} minutes.
sections.problem: Design the rate-limiting system. Cover the limit model (tiers, versioned thresholds, per-model limits per tier) and how it reaches every region; how a request's token cost is counted when its output length is unknown at admission, including streamed responses that run for a minute or more; how a team-wide limit is enforced across {{regions}} regions without a cross-region call on every request; how a tier upgrade takes effect within {{upgrade_minutes}} minutes and how you prove it did; what a 429 says (which limit, and an honest hint for when to retry); how rejections caused by a team's own limit are kept apart from refusals caused by platform overload; what each rejection records for later analysis; and the headroom view teams see.
sections.constraints: The admission check adds under 5 ms p99 to a request. Across all regions, a team never exceeds a limit by more than a bound you state (for example 5% over any minute). A region keeps admitting within its own share when it cannot reach the other regions or the coordination service. A tier upgrade is in force in every region within {{upgrade_minutes}} minutes. A retry hint is never shorter than the real wait for the limit that was hit.
sections.assumptions: Team counts, rates, tiers, thresholds and limits are hypothetical, and the rules are this exercise's (check current docs). Cumulative spend is computed by the billing system and only grows; the tier thresholds themselves are versioned and can change. Batch requests have their own limits and are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Versioned tiers, thresholds and per-model limits published as snapshots with the enforced version reported per region; requests per second checked at admission and tokens per minute reserved then settled, with a stated estimate and early release of unused reservation for long streams; team-wide limits split into regional shares with rebalancing, local decisions and a stated overshoot bound, safe behaviour when partitioned; tier upgrades traced end to end with a measured time to enforce; 429s that name the limit hit with honest, jittered retry hints; own-limit rejections kept apart from overload refusals; rejection records with team, model, region, limit type and tier version; a headroom view consistent with enforcement; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Are limits per region or global?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, per team and model across all regions combined.

clarifications.q: What counts toward tokens per minute?
clarifications.a: Input plus output tokens (this exercise's rule). The output count is known only when the response ends.

clarifications.q: Can a team's tier go down?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. A team's cumulative spend only grows, but a new threshold version can move where the boundaries are; decide what happens to teams near one.

clarifications.q: Is there a burst allowance?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say exactly what a team can send at the start of a minute, and make the headroom view agree with it.

clarifications.q: Do retried requests count again?
clarifications.a: Yes; every request that reaches admission is counted, including retries.

hints: Requests per second is known at admission; tokens per minute is not. Reserve an estimate at admission and settle it with the actual count when the response ends, returning the difference.

A team-wide limit across regions can be split into regional shares that a coordinator rebalances every few seconds from recent demand. Each region decides locally, and the overshoot is bounded by how much share can move between rebalances.
Tier state is small. Publish it as a versioned snapshot to every region, have each region report the version it enforces, and treat an upgrade as an event you can trace end to end.
followups: Walk a streamed request with 2,000 input tokens and a maximum of 8,000 output tokens through admission and completion. What is reserved, what is settled, and when is the remainder released?
A team sends all its traffic to one region while its share is spread evenly across the {{regions}} regions. How fast does the share move, and what does the team see in the meantime?
Trace a tier upgrade from the spend event to the new limit in force in every region, and show how you would prove it happened within {{upgrade_minutes}} minutes.
How do you make the retry hint honest for a tokens-per-minute limit when the wait depends on in-flight requests whose output length is still unknown?
From your data, how do you tell a team throttled by its own limit from one refused because a model was overloaded, and what does each one see?

rules.ask: That counter lives in one region. What happens to admissions in the other regions when it is 80 ms away, or unreachable for ten minutes?
Many teams set the maximum output far above what they use. How much of their tokens-per-minute budget does your reservation lock up, and what would you change?
The bucket refills every second but the limit is per minute. What burst does a team get at the start of a minute, and does your headroom view say the same?
Thousands of clients receive the same hint at the same moment. What happens when they all come back together, and how would you spread them out?
A team upgrades. How long can a region keep enforcing the old tier from that cache, and how would you know it did?

incidents: A new tier-threshold version reaches all but one of the {{regions}} regions. In that region, 1,200 teams that crossed a threshold still get their old limits 50 minutes later, well past the {{upgrade_minutes}}-minute target, and nobody is paged.

After a client library release, every tokens-per-minute rejection carries a retry hint of one second. Clients retry in lockstep, rejections reach 40% of all requests at peak, and admitted tokens stay flat.

Teams running long streamed generations report being throttled at about 35% of their tokens-per-minute limit by their own count: reservations sized by the maximum output length are held until each stream ends.

templates.title: Searching public posts as a server-side tool — a live index queried inside a response
templates.subtopic: time-partitioned index, given scoring function, deletion-safe caching, latency budgets

sections.scenario: A model API offers a server-side tool that searches public posts. During a response the model decides to call it with a query, an optional time range and optional filters such as language; the tool returns a ranked list of posts and the response cites the ones it used. About {{posts_per_day}} public posts with a given schema (post id, version, creation time, language label you are given, synthetic tokens, aggregate engagement counts) arrive each day, and the last {{searchable_days}} days are searchable. Edits arrive as new versions and deletions as events, both from an ingestion pipeline that already exists. At peak the tool is called {{calls_per_second}} times a second, and each call has a budget of {{budget_ms}} ms because the model is waiting.
sections.problem: Design the query side of the tool. Cover the index layout over time (how the newest minutes are held, how older data is organised, how partitions are retired); how a time range prunes the work; candidate retrieval and how the scoring function you are given is applied (its inputs are the match against the query, recency and the post's aggregate engagement counts); merging the top results across shards with deterministic ties; edits (only the latest version is returned) and deletions (a deleted post is never returned or cited once its deletion has been processed); any caching of results and how it stays safe under deletions; behaviour when a shard is slow (partial results, clearly marked); what each call returns to the model (post id, version, score, citation); and what is logged per call.
sections.constraints: Tool call p99 within {{budget_ms}} ms at {{calls_per_second}} calls a second. A deleted post is never returned or cited more than 30 seconds after its deletion event is received (this exercise's rule). Identical calls against the same index version return the same ranked list. Logs carry post ids and versions, never post text, and no individual author appears in any report.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, budgets and windows are hypothetical. The scoring function, its weights and the language labels are given to you and are out of scope; you decide where and how it is evaluated. Ingestion freshness is owned by another team; assume a post is handed to you within a minute of creation.
sections.criteria: Time-partitioned layout with a fresh in-memory tier, immutable older segments and whole-partition retirement; time-range pruning before any scoring; the given scoring function applied consistently with deterministic tie-breaks and a clear top-k merge; latest-version-only results with versioned citations; deletions enforced at serve time on every path including caches and replicas, with a stated bound; per-shard deadlines and explicitly marked partial results; hot-partition handling (more replicas for the newest partitions, caching of recent-window candidates, load-aware routing); per-call logs of ids, versions, timings and outcomes without post text; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Lexical, vector or both?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say what each costs at this volume and how the given score combines them.

clarifications.q: How common are time ranges?
clarifications.a: Most calls ask for the last hour or the last day; a few ask for a specific older window.

clarifications.q: May an edited post's older version be returned?
clarifications.a: No. Only the latest version, and the citation names that version.

clarifications.q: Can the tool return fewer results than asked?
clarifications.a: Yes, if it says so and why (no matches, time budget, a shard missing).

clarifications.q: Can results be cached between different teams' calls?
clarifications.a: The posts are public, so yes, if no team-specific filter or setting changes the result; say how you keep that true.

hints: Partition by time: a small, frequently rebuilt in-memory tier for the newest minutes, immutable segments for older hours and days, and whole-partition retirement at the end of the window.
Deletions are cheapest as a tombstone set checked at serve time on every result, regardless of which index or cache produced it; physical removal can come later.
A per-shard deadline turns a slow shard into a marked partial result instead of a timeout for the whole call.
followups: Walk one call asking for the last hour in one language through the system, with the time spent at each step against the {{budget_ms}} ms budget.
A post is deleted while a result list containing it sits in your cache. Show exactly why it is never returned again.
A widely discussed event makes most calls ask for the last ten minutes. Which shards get hot, and what do you change?
How do you make the merged ranking deterministic when scores tie across shards, and why does the model need that?
The scoring function is replaced by a new version. How do you roll it out, compare it with the old one, and keep citations from both versions explainable?

rules.ask: How do you keep deletions visible within 30 seconds when segments are immutable and merges run in the background?
What exactly is in the cache key, and what makes a cached list unsafe once one of its posts is deleted?
Approximate search can miss a post the exact scoring would rank first. How would you measure that, and is it acceptable for a time-range filter of the last ten minutes?
One shard of many answers in three times the usual time. What does the caller get, and how does the model learn the results are partial?
A replica lags the deletion stream by two minutes. Can a query routed to it return a deleted post, and what stops that?

incidents: A cached result list for a popular query keeps citing a post for 20 minutes after it was deleted: the cache key held the query and time range but nothing tied to deletions, and serve-time checks were skipped for cache hits.

When a widely discussed event breaks, 70% of calls ask for the last hour. The shards holding the newest partition reach 95% CPU and tool-call p99 rises to four times the {{budget_ms}} ms budget, while shards for older partitions sit idle.
One shard answers slowly after a disk fault. Because the merger waits for every shard, 8% of calls time out instead of returning the other shards' results marked partial.

templates.title: A team's usage console — spend toward the next tier, limit headroom, and numbers that match the invoice
templates.subtopic: one priced usage fact, provisional and final numbers, tier progress, tenant isolation

sections.scenario: {{teams}} teams use a model API through ordinary requests, the batch API (billed at a discount), server-side tools (each tool call billed by this exercise's rule) and regional endpoints (billed with a price multiplier). Each team's usage console shows: spend this month and spend toward the next of {{tiers}} spend tiers; current limit headroom per model; and breakdowns by model, API key, ordinary versus batch, tool and region. The platform records about {{usage_rows}} usage rows a day. Teams reconcile the console against their invoice and complain when the two disagree. The console should be no more than {{fresh_minutes}} minutes behind.
sections.problem: Design the console's data. Cover the usage record and its ids; where prices, batch discounts, tool-call charges and regional multipliers are applied (once, from versioned price data); how batch requests that finish later are dated; how the console separates provisional numbers from final, invoiced ones; how spend toward the next tier is computed so it agrees with the system that actually changes a team's tier; how limit headroom is shown from enforcement data rather than from billing data; late and duplicate usage events; the breakdowns and how they sum to the total; the tie-out that proves the closed month equals the invoice; and how one team's data never appears in another team's console.
sections.constraints: For a closed month, the console's total for a team equals the invoice to the cent, and every breakdown sums to that total. The console is at most {{fresh_minutes}} minutes behind for provisional numbers. Money is never stored or summed in floating point. A team sees only its own usage, and every view is scoped by the verified identity of the caller.
sections.assumptions: Team counts, volumes, prices, discounts, multipliers and tier thresholds are hypothetical, and the rules are this exercise's (check current docs). Usage events come from the request path with a request id, team, key, model, region, token counts, tool calls and a batch id when there is one.
sections.criteria: One priced usage fact with stable ids, the price version, discount and multiplier recorded at write time and integer minor units; one stated dating rule for batch usage applied in console, tier progress and invoice; provisional versus closed numbers labelled, with closed periods changed only by dated adjustments; tier progress read from the same definition the tier engine uses and limit headroom read from enforcement data; idempotent ingestion of late and duplicate events; breakdowns that sum to totals and a continuous tie-out against invoices; team scoping from verified identity in every query path and export; freshness measured and shown; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery, customer communication and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which spend moves a team up a tier?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, invoiced and paid spend; decide how the console shows spend that is accrued but not yet paid.

clarifications.q: When is a batch request's usage dated?
clarifications.a: Your choice between submission and completion; state it and apply it everywhere, including the invoice.

clarifications.q: Can prices change mid-month?
clarifications.a: Yes, with an effective time; requests are priced by the version in force when they were served.

clarifications.q: Are credits and refunds shown?
clarifications.a: Yes, as their own lines, so the console explains the whole invoice.

clarifications.q: Can teams export the breakdowns?
clarifications.a: Yes, and an export must match the console exactly.

hints: Price each usage row once, when it is written, with the price version, discount and multiplier recorded on the row; every view and the invoice then sum the same rows.
Keep two clocks: provisional rows that can still change, and closed periods that change only by dated adjustments. Show which one each number comes from.
Tier progress and limit headroom come from different systems. Read each from the system that enforces it, and label what each means.
followups: Walk one request that used the post-search tool twice in a regional endpoint from usage event to a line on the console and a line on the invoice.
A team's console says it passed the next tier threshold yesterday, but its limits have not changed. What happened, and what should the console have said?
A price version changes on the 15th. Show how the month's total and every breakdown still sum to the invoice.
A batch submitted at 23:50 on the last day of the month finishes at 02:10 the next day. Which month carries it, in the console, the tier progress and the invoice?
How would you prove continuously that the console and invoices agree for every team, and what do you do when one does not?

rules.ask: Where can a fraction of a cent exist in your pipeline, and where exactly is it rounded?
A late usage event arrives for an hour already rolled up. Which numbers change, and how does the team see that?
Which numbers on the console must be exact and which may be provisional, and how does the page say which is which?
A new breakdown is added by an engineer who forgets the team filter. What stops it leaking another team's usage?
The same usage event arrives twice, once late. What is the key that makes the second one harmless?

incidents: The console counts accrued spend toward the next tier while the tier engine counts paid spend, so 600 teams see a tier reached on the console that their limits do not reflect, and support tickets triple in a day.
A regional multiplier version that took effect mid-month is applied by the console to the whole month, so for teams using that region the console and the invoice differ by up to 4%.
A backlog in the usage stream leaves the console 3 hours behind, far past the {{fresh_minutes}}-minute target, and the page still labels its numbers as current.

templates.title: Citation quality monitoring — dead links, unsupported spans and per-tool trends
templates.subtopic: link checking with politeness, versioned support scores, probe sets, stratified review samples

sections.scenario: Responses that use the server-side web search or public-post search tools attach citations: a span of the response and the source (a URL, or a post id and version) that supports it. About {{citations_per_day}} citations are produced a day. The product team wants to know, per tool, model and week, how often citations point to dead links, how often a support score you are given says the source does not support its span, and whether either is getting worse. Production responses belong to the teams that made them. In this exercise only content-free signals (tool, model, time, the cited URL or post id, link status, the support score and its scorer version) leave the request path, and only teams that opted in contribute response text to review. A fixed probe set of {{probe_queries}} synthetic queries is also run every day. Each week {{sample_size}} citations go to people who judge whether the score was right.
sections.problem: Design the monitoring. Cover the citation record and what it may and may not hold; link checking (when a URL is checked, how often it is rechecked, how 404s, timeouts, server errors, redirects to a home page and blocked requests are told apart, and how small sites are not overloaded); post citations whose post was later deleted (a separate status, never a dead link, and never re-fetched); where the support score is computed and how its scorer version is recorded; the probe set and what it adds that production signals cannot; per-tool, per-model weekly trends and alerts that tell a real change from a change in the scorer or the checker; and the weekly review sample, how it is drawn and what reviewers see.
sections.constraints: No response text is kept for teams that did not opt in. The link checker sends no more than a polite, per-domain rate of requests, honours the site's crawling rules, and fetches status only, keeping no page contents. A cited URL is rechecked every {{recheck_hours}} hours while it keeps being cited. Every trend can be split by scorer version and checker version. The review sample is drawn so that rare tools and models are represented.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, rates and sizes are hypothetical, and the opt-in, retention and checking rules are this exercise's (check current docs). The support score is a function you are given: it takes a span and source text and returns a number between 0 and 1 with a version; "unsupported" means below a threshold that is also given.
sections.criteria: A citation record that holds ids, tool, model, times, link status and versioned scores but no response text outside the opt-in; a polite link checker with per-domain rate limits, crawl-rule honouring, status-only fetches, recheck scheduling and statuses that tell gone pages from blocked, transient and redirected ones; deleted posts as their own status, never re-fetched; scores computed in the request path with the scorer version and threshold recorded; a daily probe set to separate tool, model and scorer changes; trends and alerts split by scorer and checker version with seasonality handled; a stratified, reweighted review sample with written guidance and agreement measured; aggregate-only reporting; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can the score be recomputed later over production citations?
clarifications.a: Not for teams that did not opt in, because their text is not kept. It is computed once in the request path; the probe set can be rescored at any time.

clarifications.q: Is a redirect a dead link?
clarifications.a: Not by itself. A redirect to the same page's new address is live; a redirect of every path to a home page usually means the page is gone. Decide how you tell them apart.

clarifications.q: What do reviewers judge?
clarifications.a: Whether the source supports the span, on a fixed scale with written guidance. They never judge the topic of the content.

clarifications.q: Who sees the trends?
clarifications.a: The product and model teams, in aggregate. No individual team's citations appear in a report.

clarifications.q: How fresh must the trends be?
clarifications.a: Daily is enough; the dead-link rate for a tool should alert within a day.

hints: Separate three clocks: when a citation was made, when its link was last checked, and which scorer version scored it. Most false alarms come from mixing them.
A fixed probe set run every day is a controlled experiment: the queries do not change, so movements in its numbers come from the tools, the models or the scorer.
Stratify the review sample by tool, model and score band, and weight the results back to the population when you report them.
followups: Walk one web citation from the response to its first link check, its rechecks and the weekly trend it lands in.
The unsupported share doubles overnight for every tool at once. How do you find out within an hour whether the citations changed or the scorer did?
How would you check that the support score agrees with people, and what do you do if it disagrees mostly for one tool?
A cited site starts blocking the checker. What status do its citations get, and what keeps that from looking like a wave of dead links?
A model team wants the response text of unsupported citations from all teams to debug. What do you offer instead?

rules.ask: The checker hits a small site 50,000 times in an hour because a popular response cites it. What limits that, and what does the site owner see?
The judge model is updated. How do you keep last month's trend comparable with this month's?
One tool makes 2% of citations. How many of your {{sample_size}} reviews does it get, and is that enough to say anything about it?
Which fields in that record could identify a team or reveal a response, and why do you need each one?
Your dead-link alert fires every Monday because many sites are down for maintenance at the weekend. How do you make it useful?

incidents: The dead-link rate for web citations jumps from 2% to 15% in a day. A change to URL canonicalisation stripped a query parameter that some sites need, so the checker requests pages that do not exist; the cited pages are fine.

A new scorer version is deployed and the unsupported share doubles overnight across every tool and model; nothing about the citations changed, and the weekly report has already gone out with the jump.
A small site cited by a widely used response blocks the checker after a burst of requests, and all its citations are reported as dead for {{recheck_hours}} hours.

templates.title: Regional endpoints at scale — routing to the chosen region, logs kept in region, and the multiplier billed
templates.subtopic: residency settings, team-chosen failover, in-region logs, versioned price multipliers

sections.scenario: A model API is served from {{regions}} regions. Teams call either a global endpoint, which routes each request to a region, or a regional endpoint, which serves the request only in that region. About {{pinned_share}} of teams have a residency setting: their requests, request logs and usage records must stay in a chosen region. Some models are offered only in some regions. Requests served by a regional endpoint are billed at {{multiplier}} times the base price (this exercise's rule; check current docs). When a region is degraded, each team's own failover policy applies: fail the request, or move it to another region the team allowed. Moving traffic must happen within {{failover_minutes}} minutes of a region being declared degraded.
sections.problem: Design regional serving. Cover the region and model catalogue (which models each region offers, versioned); routing for the global and the regional endpoints; how a team's residency setting and failover policy are stored, versioned and enforced on every request; capacity when failover moves traffic into another region; where request logs, usage records and metrics are kept, and what may leave a region (aggregates for billing and capacity, never request-level data of a pinned team); how the price multiplier is applied by the region that actually served each request, with versioned multipliers; and how you detect and report any request that was served outside the place a team's setting allowed.
sections.constraints: A request from a team pinned to a region is never served, logged or stored outside it. Failover follows each team's chosen policy and completes within {{failover_minutes}} minutes of the declaration. Every usage record carries the region that served it and the multiplier version applied. Cross-region data for billing and capacity is aggregate only. A routing mistake that breaks a residency setting must be detected within an hour and reported to the team.
sections.assumptions: Regions, shares, multipliers and timings are hypothetical, and the residency and billing rules are this exercise's (check current docs). Each region has its own serving fleet, storage and observability stack.
sections.criteria: A versioned catalogue of regions and models; routing that resolves residency and failover policy at the edge into allowed regions carried with the request and enforced at every hop; failover by team policy with admission limits and load shedding in receiving regions; request logs, usage records and metrics kept in region with only aggregates leaving; the serving region and multiplier version recorded on every usage record and billed from it; detection of any out-of-region serving within an hour with team notification and billing correction; access controls on debugging tools that respect residency; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery, customer communication and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the global endpoint billed with the multiplier?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; only requests sent to a regional endpoint are, at the multiplier version in force when the request was served.

clarifications.q: Can a pinned team fail over?
clarifications.a: Only to regions it listed in advance; many pinned teams list none and prefer errors.

clarifications.q: Does an engineer debugging an incident get request logs from every region?
clarifications.a: Only within each region's own tools, and pinned teams' request logs never leave their region.

clarifications.q: Are models identical across regions?
clarifications.a: The same model version where offered; some regions lag new versions by days.

clarifications.q: Who declares a region degraded?
clarifications.a: Automated health checks with a human able to override; decide the signals.

hints: Make the serving region a first-class field on every request, log line and usage record, set by the region that served it, never inferred later.
Resolve the team's residency and failover policy once at the edge into a short list of allowed regions, and carry that list with the request so any later hop can refuse.
Ship only aggregates out of a region (per team, model and hour), and build global billing and capacity views from those.
followups: Walk a request from a pinned team through a regional endpoint: routing, serving, logging, usage and billing.
One region is degraded. Which teams move, where, and how do you avoid overloading the regions that receive them?
A new model version is in only two of the {{regions}} regions. What does a pinned team in a third region get when it asks for it?
The multiplier changes at midnight UTC while long streamed requests are running. Which version applies to each of them?
How would you prove to a pinned team, every month, that none of its requests were served or logged elsewhere?

rules.ask: The nearest region by network distance is not the one a pinned team chose. Where exactly does your design stop that request from being served nearby?
A pinned team's request logs would land in that central store. What is allowed to leave the region instead, and how is that enforced?
Failover moves several thousand teams into one region in {{failover_minutes}} minutes. How do you keep that region from failing next?
A request is admitted in one region and served in another after a retry. Which region's multiplier is billed, and how do you know?
A backup of a region's usage store is copied to another region for durability. Does that break a residency setting, and what would you do instead?

incidents: A region is declared degraded. Teams whose policy allows failover move to the next region, which runs out of capacity for one model within ten minutes, while pinned teams with no failover receive errors for 40 minutes; both groups say the platform failed them.
During an incident review, an engineer copies a sample of request logs from one region into a shared analysis store in another, including requests from 30 teams pinned to that region.

A routing configuration change sends 3% of a pinned team's regional-endpoint requests to another region for two hours. The responses are correct, but they are billed at the wrong region's multiplier and served outside the team's region.

templates.title: Developers say they are being throttled unfairly, and the data is ambiguous
templates.subtopic: evidence gaps, honest communication, fixing the measurement

channel: support tickets from several large teams
a widely shared post by a well-known developer
affected: most teams in one spend tier
evidence_gap: usage metrics aggregated per minute while enforcement acts per second
rejection logs kept for only three days
no record of which limit rejected each request

sections.scenario: You lead the team that owns usage and rate-limit analytics for a model API. Through {{channel}}, {{affected}} say they receive 429 rejections well below the limits published for their tier, and some say the platform is quietly favouring other customers. Your dashboards show their usage below the limits in most minutes, but you know they cannot settle the question: there is {{evidence_gap}}. The team that runs enforcement says the limiter is working as designed. Support wants something to tell people today.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover what you say publicly today, before you know the answer, and what you refuse to say; how you get evidence that can actually settle the question, given {{evidence_gap}}; how you work with the enforcement team without it becoming a blame exercise; what you do if the developers turn out to be right, partly right, or wrong; and what you change so the next complaint can be answered from data within hours. Then tell me about a real time users or another team said a system was treating them unfairly and the data did not clearly say who was right, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not own the limiter and cannot change its behaviour yourself. Any change to published limits or credits is a product and finance decision. Individual teams' usage can be discussed only with those teams, never in public.
sections.assumptions: The teams, limits and figures are hypothetical, and the limit rules are this exercise's (check current docs).
sections.criteria: Communicates early and honestly (acknowledges, says what is being checked and when the next update comes) without claiming certainty either way; identifies why the existing data cannot settle the question and gets evidence at the resolution enforcement uses, starting from exact cases with the teams' permission; checks for differences by tier, region and model rather than assuming fairness; works with the enforcement team on shared evidence rather than blame; has a plan for each outcome, including owning a platform fault publicly and taking credits to the people who decide them; protects other teams' data; changes the data kept (rejection records with limit type, per-second resolution, longer retention) so the next question is answered quickly; real example with what they personally did and what settled it, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is there any sign the limiter treats teams differently?
clarifications.a: Not that you know of, but nobody has checked by tier or by region.

clarifications.q: Could the teams' own clients be the cause?
clarifications.a: Possibly: retries count as requests, and streamed responses hold token budget. You do not know how much this explains.

clarifications.q: How quickly do people want an answer?
clarifications.a: The thread is growing; support wants a statement today and the enforcement lead wants to wait for a full analysis.

clarifications.q: Can you contact affected teams directly?
clarifications.a: Yes, through support, with their permission to look at their own usage.

hints: Separate what you can say now (what you know, what you are checking, when you will report back) from what needs evidence.
Reconstruct a few affected teams' traffic at the resolution enforcement uses before you generalise; a handful of exact cases beats an average.
Plan for each outcome in advance: right, partly right, wrong. Each needs its own message and its own fix.
followups: Draft the two or three sentences support posts today. What do you deliberately leave out?
The enforcement lead says the limiter is correct and the developers misread the docs. How do you respond?
The data shows half the rejections came from the teams' own retry storms and half from a real bug that hit one region. What do you say publicly, and to whom first?
What would you change in the data you keep so that the next complaint like this can be answered in hours?
In your real example, what evidence finally settled it, and did you change your own mind along the way?

rules.ask: Suppose that is true for most of them. What would a developer need to see to believe it, and how would you show them without exposing other teams?
You do not own credits. What evidence would you bring to the people who do, and what would you recommend?
What exactly would you say before the analysis is done, and how do you avoid a statement you later have to retract?
Your metric says they were below the limit. At what resolution does enforcement decide, and does your metric see the same thing?
What did you personally do or decide, and when?

templates.title: Launch-day traffic far above the forecast, and what you cut to stay up
templates.subtopic: load shedding by priority, protecting commitments, communication under pressure

constrained: serving capacity for the new model
query capacity of the public-post search index
the token-accounting service behind rate limits

sections.scenario: A new model and a new server-side search feature launch together on a model API. In the {{hour}} hour after launch, traffic is {{multiple}} the forecast and the bottleneck is {{constrained}}. Latency is climbing for every customer, including teams with existing production workloads on older models, error rates are rising, and the batch queue is growing. You are the senior engineer leading the incident. Several things could be cut or degraded: new-model access for new teams, the search feature's freshness, batch processing, the usage console's freshness, free-tier traffic, and analytics pipelines that share the same infrastructure.
sections.problem: Walk me through the next three hours. Cover how you establish what is actually saturated and what is merely slow; the order in which you would cut or degrade things, and the reasoning behind that order; who decides each cut and how fast; how you protect existing production workloads and commitments; what you tell customers, and when; how you avoid cuts you cannot undo; and what you do the following week. Then tell me about a real time demand far exceeded what a system you were responsible for was built for, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Adding capacity takes hours at best. Product and marketing want the launch to remain visibly available. Some customers have contractual terms (all hypothetical here) and others are on a free tier. Any change to published limits must be stated publicly.
sections.assumptions: Traffic, forecasts, tiers and terms are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Establishes the real bottleneck from data before cutting; states a protection order (existing production workloads, correctness of billing and accounting, commitments) and cuts in a reasoned order with explicit, reversible measures first; is clear about decision rights and moves quickly within them; keeps degradations visible to customers and to the model (labelled delayed results, explicit errors) rather than silent; watches the clocks of anything paused; communicates early on a cadence; follows up with capacity planning, load tests and pre-agreed shedding plans; real example with what they personally decided and what they would change, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the forecast wrong or is traffic abusive?
clarifications.a: Mostly real usage; a share looks like automated retries from a few clients.

clarifications.q: Can batch processing be paused?
clarifications.a: Yes; batch has its own completion window (this exercise's rule), so a pause is safe up to a point.

clarifications.q: Can the search feature return older results?
clarifications.a: Yes, with a freshness cost that the model would not know about unless told.

clarifications.q: Who is on the incident?
clarifications.a: Serving, search, billing and support leads; product leadership wants hourly updates.

hints: Rank what you protect before you rank what you cut: existing production workloads and data correctness usually come first.
Prefer cuts that are explicit and reversible (lower limits for new teams, pause batch within its window, label search results as delayed) over silent degradation.
Billing and usage accounting must stay correct even when the console is behind; decide what may lag and what may not.
followups: Which three things do you cut first, in what order, and why that order?
Product leadership asks you to keep new-model access open to everyone and degrade older models instead. What do you say?
You pause batch processing. How do you make sure no batch misses its completion window without anyone noticing?
What do customers hear in the first hour, and from whom?
In your real example, what did you cut, and what would you cut differently now?

rules.ask: Capacity arrives in four hours at best. What do you do in the meantime, minute by minute?
Lowering limits is a public change. Which teams does it hit, how do they find out, and how do you raise them again?
Cutting free traffic is simple. What does it cost you in trust, and how would you say it?
How long can batch stay paused before the completion window is at risk, and who watches that clock?
Which decisions did you make yourself, and which did you take to someone else?

templates.title: Sorting decisions you can undo from ones you cannot, under extreme time pressure
templates.subtopic: reversibility, cost of undoing, making decisions cheaper to reverse

situation: a storage cluster holding request logs and usage records will be full in a few hours
a pricing change must ship tonight for a launch tomorrow morning
a region is failing during a launch and traffic must move

sections.scenario: You lead {{team_size}} engineers on a model API's data platform. The situation: {{situation}}. You have about {{time}} before the decisions must be made. In front of you are proposals from the team, including: delete the oldest partitions of a dataset to free space; raise every team's rate limits temporarily; change the format of a field in a public API response; publish a public statement with numbers; change how a usage field is computed for billing; send all traffic for one model to a single region; and turn off a non-critical pipeline.
sections.problem: How do you decide what to decide quickly and what to slow down? Cover how you sort these proposals by how hard they are to undo and what undoing would cost; which ones you delegate to the team and which you take yourself or escalate; how you make a hard-to-undo decision cheaper to reverse before you make it (a snapshot, a flag, a staged rollout, a version); what evidence you insist on for the irreversible ones even under pressure; and how you record what was decided and why. Then tell me about a real time you made, or watched someone make, a decision under time pressure that could not be undone, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Some decisions affect customers' code (public API formats), money (billing fields) or data that cannot be recovered (deleted partitions). Escalation is possible, but whoever you escalate to has only minutes to give you.
sections.assumptions: The situation, team and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Sorts decisions by cost and possibility of undoing, and by who bears the cost (customers' code, money, unrecoverable data), not by how urgent they feel; delegates reversible decisions quickly with clear boundaries; slows down on irreversible ones with the minimum evidence needed (which partitions are backed up, who parses the field), and escalates them with a crisp ask; makes decisions cheaper to undo before making them (snapshot, additive field, timestamped billing change, flags, staged traffic moves); records decisions and reasons as they happen; reviews afterwards; real example with what was or was not reversible and what they learned, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is there a backup of the oldest partitions?
clarifications.a: Some of them; nobody is sure which.

clarifications.q: Do customers parse the field whose format would change?
clarifications.a: Probably; you do not know how many.

clarifications.q: Can the billing computation change be applied only to new usage?
clarifications.a: Yes, if someone builds that; it would take an hour.

clarifications.q: Who can approve a public statement?
clarifications.a: Communications and a product lead; both are reachable.

hints: For each proposal ask: if this is wrong, what does undoing it cost, who bears that cost, and can it be undone at all?

Many decisions that look irreversible can be made reversible cheaply: snapshot before deleting, add a new field instead of changing one, apply a billing change only from a timestamp, ship behind a flag.
Speed and care are not opposites: decide the reversible ones fast and spend your scarce time on the few that are not.
followups: Sort the proposals in front of you. Which do you let the team decide on their own right now?
The storage cluster will be full in two hours, and deleting the oldest partitions is the fastest fix. What do you do first?
Someone argues that changing the API field format is "just a small fix". How do you decide, and what would you do instead?
How do you record the decisions made in those hours so that someone can review them next week?
In your real example, was the decision really irreversible, and what would have made it cheaper to undo?

rules.ask: Before that runs, what is the cheapest thing that would let you undo it, and how long does it take?
Your manager has five minutes. What exactly do you bring, and what decision do you ask for?
Which of these proposals cannot be put behind a flag, and what do you do with those?
Which one of these would you most regret doing quickly, and why?
Which decision did you personally make, and what did you know when you made it?

templates.title: Developer documentation that was wrong, and customers who built on it
templates.subtopic: correcting docs, choosing which behaviour wins, migration and communication

wrong_fact: batch results would be returned in the order the requests were submitted
the tokens counted toward a tokens-per-minute limit were input tokens only
every citation returned by the search tool would include a URL
usage records would be final within one hour

sections.scenario: Your team owns part of a model API's developer documentation. You discover that for {{weeks}} weeks a page has said that {{wrong_fact}}. That was never how the system behaved. It appears that {{builders}} have built on the documented behaviour: some have code that assumes it, and a few have filed bugs that support closed as "working as intended". Changing the system to match the docs is possible but costly; changing the docs to match the system will break the assumption some customers rely on.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you confirm what the system actually does and who is affected; how you decide whether the system or the documentation changes (or both); how and when you correct the page, and what the correction says; how you reach the affected teams and library maintainers, and what help you offer; what happens to the bugs that support closed; and what you change so that documentation and behaviour cannot drift apart again. Then tell me about a real time you found that something you or your team had published was wrong after others relied on it, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot see what customers' code does, only how they call the API. The documentation is public, and any change is visible to everyone. Changing system behaviour needs the owning team's agreement and its own rollout.
sections.assumptions: The documentation, teams and figures are hypothetical; nothing here describes real documentation.
sections.criteria: Confirms the actual behaviour and the extent of reliance from evidence before acting; decides between changing docs or system by harm to affected customers and states the trade-off; corrects the page visibly with a dated note of what changed and why; reaches affected teams and library maintainers directly with concrete help (examples, a migration path, a grace period where possible); reopens and answers the bugs support closed and owns the mistake without blaming support; fixes the process (docs reviewed against shipped behaviour, executable examples or contract tests, an owner per page); real example with what they personally did and how it landed, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How did the error get in?
clarifications.a: The page was written from a design document before the feature shipped, and nobody compared it with the final behaviour.

clarifications.q: Do you know who relies on it?
clarifications.a: Partly: from support tickets, public code that calls the API, and request patterns.

clarifications.q: Is anyone harmed today?
clarifications.a: Some teams may be mis-sizing requests or mismatching results; you do not yet know how many or how badly.

clarifications.q: Does support want to reopen the closed bugs?
clarifications.a: Support is embarrassed and would rather just fix the page quietly.

hints: A quiet fix to a public page is itself a change people rely on; say what changed and why.
Decide which behaviour wins by the harm each choice does to the people affected, not by which is cheaper for you.
The root cause is a process that let docs and behaviour drift; fix that, not only the page.
followups: What does the correction on the page say, word for word, near the top?
Support wants to fix the page quietly. What do you say?
How would you find the affected teams and client libraries, and what would you offer them?
What would you put in place so that a documented behaviour is tested against the real system?
In your real example, how did the people who had relied on the mistake react, and what did you learn?

rules.ask: A team notices the page changed under them a week later. What do they conclude about every other page?
Who else relies on today's behaviour, perhaps without knowing it, and what happens to them?
Who actually reads that? How do you reach the teams whose code is affected?
Which statements on a documentation page can be tested automatically, and who owns the tests when they fail?
What did you personally do or decide?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a model API with real-time search and spend-based limits
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, limits enforced across regions, freshness and deletion, usage to the cent

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: rate limits per team enforced across several regions with a stated overshoot bound
public posts searchable within a minute of creation and never returned after deletion
usage priced once and shown to each team to the cent, matching the invoice
every request served, logged and billed only in the region a team chose
scale: hundreds of thousands of requests a second
a billion new public posts a day

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for a model API with real-time search over public posts and spend-based rate limits, at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The model API setting is hypothetical, and any limits or prices mentioned are this exercise's rules (check current docs).
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example regional shares of a team's limit with rebalancing and a stated bound; a time-partitioned index with serve-time deletion checks on every path; one priced usage fact in integer units with a continuous tie-out; residency enforced at every hop with the serving region recorded on every record); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be an API, search or billing system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the re-examination, start from one request or one post: where it enters, which ids and timestamps it carries, and which of them the new requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
What in your cache could outlive a deletion or a limit change, and how long could it be wrong?
Where in your system could a fraction of a cent appear, and where exactly is it rounded?
Which data in your system crossed regions, and could you have kept a customer's requests and logs in one region if asked?
